brief.topic: Which Pairings Make the Largest Total?

s01: Two lists contain one, two, three and two, four, six.
Pair one number from each list, multiply each pair, and add.
Which pairing gives the largest total?
Start by matching small with large.
One times six, two times four, three times two.
The total is twenty.
Now exchange the partners of the smallest and largest numbers.
One gets two.
Three gets six.
The middle pair stays still.
The total becomes twenty eight.
The gain is not an accident.
The difference between three and one is two.
The difference between six and two is four.
Their product is eight, exactly the gain from the exchange.
In general, two pairs improve when the larger first number gets the larger second number.
The gain is the product of the two differences, so it cannot be negative.
Keep removing reversed pairs and both lists end up in the same order.
That arrangement maximizes the sum of products.
Opposite orders minimize it.
If two numbers in either exchanged pair are equal, one difference is zero.
Swapping then changes nothing.
The rule comes from a local exchange we can see, repeated until no helpful exchange remains.

scenes.narration:
Two lists contain one, two, three and two, four, six. Pair one number from each list, multiply each pair, and add. Which pairing gives the largest total?

Start by matching small with large. One times six, two times four, three times two. The total is twenty.

Now exchange the partners of the smallest and largest numbers. One gets two. Three gets six. The middle pair stays still. The total becomes twenty eight.

The gain is not an accident. The difference between three and one is two. The difference between six and two is four. Their product is eight, exactly the gain from the exchange.

In general, two pairs improve when the larger first number gets the larger second number. The gain is the product of the two differences, so it cannot be negative.

Keep removing reversed pairs and both lists end up in the same order. That arrangement maximizes the sum of products. Opposite orders minimize it.

If two numbers in either exchanged pair are equal, one difference is zero. Swapping then changes nothing. The rule comes from a local exchange we can see, repeated until no helpful exchange remains.
